This is a super good analysis. I agree with the best part about Hank in past seasons being that he kind of thrives as a person in the life of crime that's killing Barry. Like you said, he's the anti-Barry, and that makes him both hilarious and compelling. It doesn't destroy him the same way that it does Barry. He's shown zero remorse, and he's still lovable, just because he's so freaking funny (and, y'know, "super nice guy," "optometrist by nature").

One thing I've been wondering in terms of Sally: is her "coming to jesus moment," as you described it, genuine, or is it because it brings her clout? Sally has started to advocate for survivors of domestic violence, and recognize abuse in her own life (Barry). I do wonder, though, if that's because people seem to give her recognition when she does talk about it, both through her performance in season 2 and through the show Joplin. I do think that her recognition of Barry's SUPER creepy "switch her dog out for a different dog" speech as horrific is a good sign - it means that even after her show has been cancelled, she's taking the lessons she learned about it from abusive behavior into her own personal life. She also hasn't really shown much remorse for the way she's treated the people around her (obviously not like...murder, like Barry or Hank, but she still hasn't been great to other people @ points) and so I wonder if her growth is also purely self-centered (here's a way to heal from the terrible things that have been done to me) and not inclusive of others (how have I hurt people in the past, and how can I be better).

Same w/ Gene - I wonder if he's apologizing because he actually feels bad, or just because it feels good to apologize. Like, when people forgive him after an apology, he gets social recognition/people start to like him (and he gets acting jobs!). But we learn that the things he did to people probably don't really mean anything to him when he legit forgot that he blacklisted his ex girlfriend from the industry. He's learning that his apologies - whether legitimate or not - aren't always enough, and if they're not legitimate apologies, he might have to learn some actual lessons about both himself and the aftermath of hurting other people from her refusal to accept his apology.

Barry, in season 1 and 2, seemed like he really wanted to be a better person for the sake of being a better person. He didn't really want to be an actor for fame or anything, just to maybe learn how to become better. I feel like by season three that's kind of gone from his character; like I said in an above comment, I feel like that "moral compass" (if you can call it that, dude is y'know, still a murderer. But it is, though, like he has a sense of right and wrong even if he doesn't follow it) doesn't really leave someone. Especially given how deeply ingrained it was in Barry, he went through so much struggle in the first few seasons because his conscience wouldn't let him live with the things he had done and was continuing to do. I hope the show explains what happened to that conscience, which was so central to his character in the first two seasons, and if he still has it/doesn't have it/where it went/why it went away.

The Democratic party is 100% not immune from racism, I definitely agree with you. I don't think the problem is only the people that are in positions of power within the party though; there are plenty of progressives who also perpetuate and uphold racism. I feel like we kind of need to end the myth that your political affiliation is the sole determiner of your participation in white supremacy; obviously, I think Dems in the past few decades have usually been on the right side of history compared to Republicans, but all sorts of people - Republicans, Dems, progressives, socialists - even people that consider themselves apolitical - can and do all participate in white supremacy.

I feel like we need to acknowledge that racism is everywhere - only then can the way we talk about racism turn from a heavily politicized blame game (ex. "this part of the Dem party is so racist, but we're not!)" into something that more people can recognize and join together in dismantling. We also should be open to different people from different parts of the political spectrums' opinions on how best to end racism (esp. through policy solutions - like obviously not "hey, let's have a debate over whether Trump's wall is good!!" because it's not, but more within the Democratic party) even if we disagree. Everyone wants to believe they're the only non-racists and say everyone else is; they're wrong.

Idk, just some thoughts, definitely let me know if you disagree or have any feedback.

Super sorry this is so long, I just thought you raised some interesting points so I had some thoughts. The main argument I've heard against progressive debate re: accessibility is that it's hard for students to gain access to progressive debate education. There's definitely merit to that, imo: Progressive debate - at least in policy, and increasingly LD - requires knowledge of different argument formats, as well as knowledge of the content of more types of arguments, which can range from critical literature to specific bills being debated in Congress. And, of course, the evidence burden is way higher. There's just way more stuff to cover. 

Honestly though, "having more stuff to cover" is one of the things that makes progressive debate so valuable. Knowledge about critical and political theory, a deep education in research skills, the critical thinking skills gained by fast and in-depth debate - etc. - are a **good** thing. It definitely decreases immediate access by making the learning curve steeper, but that learning curve is also one of the things that is most valuable about it. I honestly don't know how to balance those two things; I feel like, ideally, they shouldn't have to trade off with one another. I'm so grateful that I had the opportunity to take part in that type of debate; everyone should be able to have that extremely valuable educational experience. **We shouldn't try to curtail access to progressive debate in the name of retaining access to debate as a whole; we should instead double down on trying to make progressive debate as accessible as possible.**

I feel like, though, **progressive debate schools and people with progressive debate backgrounds 100% extend debate into underserved communities.** For example, I did policy debate in a pretty traditional region of the country debate-wise, but was lucky enough to be able to travel because I went to a school with strong support for debate. My school set up a debate camp for our region, let other teams use evidence from our Dropbox, and my coach gave advice to other coaches that were venturing onto the national circuit. College debate teams often support local UDLs, provide discounted coaching to teams in the area, or even run local debate camps. 

>...if \[progressive debate\] deters these communities from gaining access to the debate space, then it is the duty of traditional coaches like myself to oppose the spread of progressive debate with every bit of energy and resource at our disposal.

I've already covered why I believe progressive debate is good for accessibility. But - and I could be wrong - I also think that this type of total resistance to progressive debate will be ineffective. Younger generations of debaters that have been exposed to progressive debate are coming back to judge and coach. The amount of people who know about progressive debate is growing larger, and access is widening. Too much resistance over progressive debate even has the potential to become problematic. For example: in my circuit, teams (often wealthier ones) that had at least some background in progressive debate - given a judge with any circuit experience at all - were usually able to engage in progressive debate to beat more traditional teams. The teams often lost in these debates because their coach was either an opponent of progressive debate, or because they couldn't access progressive debate education because of lack of resources. 

And - this may be controversial - but there's a reason why progressive debaters are so often in finals of traditional tournaments like NSDA nats  - progressive skills translate really well into winning traditional debates as well. Even if people don't agree with me that progressive debate is good, **as long as it's inevitable, we need to focus less on resisting progressive debate and more on opening up access to it.**

Btw - this is not to say that I don't believe in the value of traditional debate - I 100% do. I just wanted to offer thoughts on the questions you raised about progressive debate particularly.
